nameStory: The Lesser Anglewing gets its name from the distinctive angular shape of its wings, which meet at sharp angles rather than smooth curves like many other katydids. It's called 'lesser' because it's smaller than its close relative, the Greater Anglewing, though both share those characteristic pointed wing edges that make them look like tiny green fighter jets.
description: The Lesser Anglewing is a bright green katydid about the size of your thumb, with distinctively pointed, angular wings that give it a geometric appearance. Like other katydids, it's a plant-eating insect related to grasshoppers and crickets, but it lives primarily in trees and shrubs rather than on the ground. Its body is flattened from side to side, and it has long, thread-like antennae that can be twice as long as its body. These nocturnal musicians are part of the summer symphony you hear in New England's trees after dark.

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Wings have sharp, angular edges that feel stiff and papery to the touch, meeting at distinct points rather than gentle curves

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length about 1-1.5 inches, noticeably smaller than the Greater Anglewing when seen side by side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright leaf-green coloration that may fade to yellowish-green, perfectly matching the foliage where it hides

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, thin antennae that feel like fine wire and constantly wave about as the insect explores

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compressed laterally (flattened side-to-side) like it's been gently squeezed, unlike the rounder grasshoppers

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Long, spiny legs that grip bark and leaves firmly, with the hind legs being particularly robust for jumping

habitat: Lesser Anglewings live in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, preferring the canopy of oak, maple, and other broadleaf trees. You'll find them in wooded areas from sea level to moderate elevations, including forest edges, parks, and mature suburban landscapes with plenty of trees. They favor areas with dense foliage that provides both food and camouflage during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically active yet, as they overwinter as eggs laid in tree bark the previous fall.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults emerge, feed, and begin calling at night. Listen for their distinctive buzzing calls after dark in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue calling and mating into early fall, with females laying eggs in bark crevices before the first hard frost ends their season.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, tucked safely in bark crevices where they'll wait until the following summer to hatch.

funFact: Lesser Anglewings are ventriloquists of the insect world - their calls seem to come from everywhere and nowhere at once because sound bounces off leaves in complex ways, making it nearly impossible to pinpoint exactly which tree the singer is in even when you're standing right underneath it.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Greater Anglewing, but the Lesser is noticeably smaller and has slightly different wing proportions. Memory trick: 'Lesser' means smaller - if you can cup it comfortably in your palm, it's likely the Lesser Anglewing.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'katydids,' not all species in this family actually make the classic 'katy-did' sound - Anglewings produce more of a continuous buzzing or rattling call that's quite different from the rhythmic 'katy-did-katy-didn't' of their more famous relatives.
compareHints: The Lesser Anglewing is smaller and more delicate than its close relative the Greater Anglewing, with proportionally narrower wings and a more slender build. Both share the distinctive angular wing shape, but the Greater Anglewing is notably more robust and has broader wings. When comparing to other katydids in the region, Anglewings stand out immediately because of their sharp-edged, geometric wing shape versus the more rounded or oval wings of most other species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Greater Anglewing is significantly larger than its relative the Lesser Anglewing and has more dramatically angled, diamond-shaped wings.
